chapterTitle: Deploying Fabric on Kubernetes (K8s) - Part 2: Fabric CA and Orderer Deployment

screens.title: Fabric CA and Orderer Deployment on Kubernetes
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to deploy the two foundational services of a production Hyperledger Fabric network on Kubernetes: the Fabric Certificate Authority and a Raft-based Orderer cluster. We will focus on the practical Kubernetes primitives you need — Persistent Volume Claims for durability, Secrets for private keys, Deployments or StatefulSets where they belong, and Services for networking. You will see concrete YAML snippets and a live workflow for creating crypto material, encoding keys, creating Secrets, and applying manifests. Understanding these components matters because identity and ordering are the backbone of Fabric: if a CA loses its database or an Orderer loses its ledger state, the network can become inconsistent or fail. A common misconception is that everything can be ephemeral in Kubernetes; for Fabric it cannot — cryptographic materials and ledgers must be persistent and carefully handled. By the end you will know which Kubernetes object to use for each need, how to provide the CA and Orderer with their certificates, and how to validate they started correctly. Ready to explore the key topics and practical steps that follow?

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › Overview
Fabric CA and Orderer Deployment on Kubernetes
Secure, persistent, and highly available identity and ordering services for a production Fabric network.
Why this matters
Identity and ordering are critical: CAs issue the certificates you trust, and Orderers maintain the ledger and consensus. On Kubernetes you must design manifests to keep crypto material durable and private while enabling Raft to maintain consensus across stable identities.
Focus areas
Persistent volumes for CA databases and orderer ledgers, secure Secrets for private keys, StatefulSets for Raft orderers, and correct Service types for connectivity.
Explore Key Topics
Fabric CA
Deploy with a PVC and supply private keys via Secrets, then enroll peers and orderers with fabric-ca-client.
Raft Orderer
Use StatefulSets for stable hostnames and per-pod PVCs. Pre-generate MSP/TLS and mount via Secrets and ConfigMaps.
Troubleshooting
Check env vars, Secret mounts, consenters lists and genesis.block. Use kubectl logs and describe to diagnose issues.
Visual concept
CA Pod + PVC
Persistent store for CA database and root crypto
Raft Orderer StatefulSet
Stable hostnames, per-pod PVCs, and consensus
Coming up: hands-on creation of Secrets, PVCs, CA Deployment YAML, and conceptual Orderer StatefulSet manifests.
Starter checklist

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to design Kubernetes manifests and deploy Fabric Certificate Authorities and a Raft-based Orderer cluster with production considerations. You will learn to persist CA and Orderer data using Persistent Volume Claims, protect private keys using Kubernetes Secrets, and choose the appropriate workload object — Deployment for a single CA instance and StatefulSet for a Raft Orderer cluster. You'll also be able to prepare and mount MSP and TLS materials using Secrets and ConfigMaps, register and enroll identities using the fabric-ca-client workflow, and validate deployments using kubectl logs and describe. For example, you will practice base64 encoding a CA private key, create the Secret manifest, apply a PVC manifest, and launch a CA Deployment that mounts both. This competency ensures your network has durable identity management and a stable ordering backbone.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives describe the hands-on skills you'll practice. First, you'll create a base64 representation of a CA private key and put it into a Kubernetes Secret so the CA Pod can access its key at runtime without embedding it in YAML. Second, you'll create a Persistent Volume Claim and mount it into the CA Pod so the CA database and generated certificates survive restarts. Third, you'll design a StatefulSet manifest for a Raft Orderer cluster that gives each pod a stable hostname and its own PVC for ledger data, crucial for consensus. Finally, you'll perform validation steps: check pods with kubectl get pods -l, inspect logs for the CA server startup message, and verify the ORDERER_CONSENSUS_RAFT_CONSENTERS list matches stable hostnames and TLS certificates. These tasks matter because they reduce downtime, prevent accidental exposure of private keys, and allow Raft to form a stable cluster. Each skill maps to an exam-style competency: persistent storage, secrets management, StatefulSet design, and troubleshooting.

screens.title: Fabric CA: Purpose and deployment model
screens.narratorSegment: A Fabric Certificate Authority issues and manages the cryptographic identities used by peers, orderers, and client applications. It maintains a database of registered identities and issues X.509 certificates when clients enroll. In Kubernetes, the CA must persist both its database and any root crypto material so that restarts do not lose identity state. Typically, a single CA instance for an organization can run as a Deployment, because it does not require a stable network identity for consensus like a Raft Orderer does. However, the CA does need persistent storage: mount a Persistent Volume Claim into the CA container at the server home path so the database and generated certs survive Pod termination. A concrete example is defining a PVC requesting 1Gi and mounting it at /etc/hyperledger/fabric-ca-server, which keeps SQLite or PostgreSQL files and the root certificate across restarts. A common misconception is that Secrets alone provide persistence; they do not — Secrets secure small pieces of data but your CA's database and generated TLS cert files require a PVC. Key takeaway: use a Deployment for CA lifecycle, PVC for persistence, and Secrets for private key handling so your CA remains both durable and secure. How will you confirm the CA retained its database after a restart?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Fabric CA issues identities and must persist its database and crypto materials on a PVC when deployed in Kubernetes.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › Fabric CA: Purpose
What the Fabric CA provides
  • Registration and enrollment of identities via fabric-ca-client.
  • Storage of identity database and issued certificates.
  • TLS certificate generation for components when enabled.
Concrete example
Define a PVC requesting 1Gi and mount it into the CA at /etc/hyperledger/fabric-ca-server so the SQLite DB and certs persist across Pod restarts.
Key Takeaway

Use a PVC for CA state; Deployments are acceptable for single-instance CAs, but storage must be persistent and the private key kept in a Secret.

Common misconception
Treating Secrets as a persistence mechanism. Secrets protect small sensitive values but do not replace a PVC for databases and filesystem artifacts the CA writes during operation.
Check your understanding
Why mount the CA data directory to persistent storage?
What would happen if a CA lost its database after restart?

screens.title: Persistent Volume Claims for CA and Orderer
screens.narratorSegment: Persistent Volume Claims are the Kubernetes primitive you use to request durable storage from the cluster. For Fabric components this is essential: CA databases and Orderer ledgers must survive Pod restarts. The typical flow is: create a PVC manifest specifying access mode and requested storage, apply it, and reference the claim in your Deployment or StatefulSet volume mounts. For a CA you might request 1Gi and mount it at /etc/hyperledger/fabric-ca-server; for each Orderer in a StatefulSet you provide a per-pod PVC for ledger files. A concrete example from our chapter shows a ca-org1-pvc. yaml requesting 1Gi and ReadWriteOnce access mode. After applying the PVC, verify it bound to a PersistentVolume with kubectl get pvc. Common mistakes include insufficient storage size, wrong accessModes, or lacking a StorageClass in the cluster, which prevents binding. Another gotcha: using a single shared PVC for multiple Orderer pods will break Raft because each Orderer needs its own dedicated ledger storage. Key takeaway: match the PVC scope to the component — shared for stateless items only, per-pod for stateful ledgers. When you create a StatefulSet for Orderers, ensure the volumeClaimTemplates produce separate PVCs for each replica.

keyIdea.title: Process summary
keyIdea.text: Create a PVC per stateful component, ensure it binds, and mount it in the pod to retain database and ledger files across restarts.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › PVC Process
Step-by-step
  1. Create a PVC YAML with accessModes and resources.requests.storage.
  2. Apply it with kubectl apply -f ca-org1-pvc.yaml and confirm binding via kubectl get pvc.
  3. Reference the claimName in your Deployment or use volumeClaimTemplates in a StatefulSet for per-pod PVCs.
  4. Mount the PVC to the component's data path (e.g., /etc/hyperledger/fabric-ca-server or /var/hyperledger/production/orderer).
Example PVC
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: ca-org1-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
Key Takeaway

Use per-pod PVCs for stateful Orderers and a dedicated PVC for each CA to ensure each component keeps its local state.

Common mistakes
  • Expecting Secrets to persist generated files — they do not.
  • Using a single shared PVC across multiple stateful replicas.
  • Omitting a StorageClass in clusters where dynamic provisioning is required.
Check with kubectl get pvc and kubectl describe pvc to ensure your claim bound correctly and that the underlying PV has enough capacity.

screens.title: Securing the CA private key with a Kubernetes Secret
screens.narratorSegment: Handling the CA private key securely is non-negotiable. The recommended pattern is to pre-generate or locate the CA's private key on a secure host, base64 encode its contents, and create a Kubernetes Secret that can be mounted as a file into the CA Pod. This keeps the key out of cleartext YAML and avoids accidental commits. The chapter provides an example workflow: find the CA private key produced by cryptogen, run a base64 encode command, and populate a Secret manifest with the resulting value. After creating the Secret, reference it in the Deployment volumes list and mount the key path into the CA server expected TLS key location. A concrete command example is to run cat | base64 -w 0 on a machine that holds the key, then place that value under data in a Secret manifest. A common slip is to place keys in ConfigMaps or in container images: neither is secure. Another mistake is failing to set the volume mount as readOnly, which increases risk. After deployment, verify the CA Pod reads the key and starts, looking for the 'Starting CA server' message in logs. Key takeaway: Secrets are the Kubernetes primitive designed for this purpose; use them with readOnly mounts and proper RBAC to restrict access. How would you confirm the Secret is mounted and used by the CA server?

keyIdea.title: Secure handling
keyIdea.text: Pre-generate or retrieve the private key, base64 encode it, create a Secret, mount it read-only into the CA container, and verify startup logs.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › CA Secret Walkthrough
Example Secret creation steps
# On a secure host locate the CA private key
cat <path-to-org1-ca-private-key> | base64 -w 0

# Then create a Secret manifest using the base64 value
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: ca-org1-key
type: Opaque
data:
  ca.org1.example.com-key.pem: <base64_encoded_key>
Apply this with kubectl apply -f ca-org1-secret.yaml and then reference the secret in your Deployment volumes so the file appears at the TLS key path inside the Pod.
Mounting pattern
In the Pod spec declare a volume of type secret pointing to the secretName, then volumeMount the specific path and mark it readOnly: true. This reduces the risk of accidental modification and limits attack surface.
Check
After deploying, run kubectl logs <ca-pod> and look for the CA startup message. If TLS key paths are wrong the CA will error and logs will indicate missing file or permission issues.

screens.title: Deploying the Fabric CA: a manifest walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: A CA Deployment manifest brings together configuration, Secrets, and persistent storage. Key sections to check are metadata and labels for service selectors, env vars for FABRIC_CA_HOME and TLS configuration, ports for both CA and operations endpoints, and volumeMounts that bind the PVC and Secret to the correct paths. The example manifest in the chapter shows env vars like FABRIC_CA_SERVER_CA_NAME and FABRIC_CA_SERVER_TLS_ENABLED, ports 7054 and 9443, a PVC volume called ca-org1-data, and a secret volume for the TLS key. When you craft this manifest, confirm the secretName matches the Secret you created and that the filename inside the secret matches the env var FABRIC_CA_SERVER_TLS_KEYFILE path. Also ensure the PVC claimName matches the PVC you applied earlier. A concrete example: after applying ca-org1-deployment. yaml you should run kubectl get pods -l org=org1 and kubectl logs to confirm the CA announces it is starting. A common mistake is mismatched file names between the Secret data key and the env var pointing to the TLS keyfile; that will produce a startup error. Key takeaway: align env vars, Secret filenames, volume names, and PVC claim names precisely so the CA has the configuration and materials it expects.

keyIdea.title: Manifest alignment
keyIdea.text: Ensure env vars, Secret filenames, PVC claim names, and volumeMount paths are consistent to let the CA start with its TLS key and persistent data.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › CA Deployment Walkthrough
Essential manifest sections
  • env: pass FABRIC_CA_HOME, FABRIC_CA_SERVER_CA_NAME, FABRIC_CA_SERVER_TLS_ENABLED, and TLS file path envs.
  • ports: expose 7054 (CA) and 9443 (operations) as shown in examples.
  • volumeMounts: mount the PVC to the CA data directory and the Secret to the TLS key path as readOnly.
  • volumes: reference the PVC claimName and the Secret name exactly as created.
Snippet (volume reference)
volumes:
  - name: ca-org1-data
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: ca-org1-pvc
  - name: ca-org1-tls-key
    secret:
      secretName: ca-org1-key

volumeMounts:
  - name: ca-org1-data
    mountPath: /etc/hyperledger/fabric-ca-server
  - name: ca-org1-tls-key
    mountPath: /etc/hyperledger/fabric-ca-server/tls-key
    readOnly: true
Validation checklist
  1. kubectl get pods -l org=org1
  2. kubectl logs <ca-pod-name> and search for startup lines
  3. kubectl describe pod <ca-pod-name> to verify volume mounts
If the CA reports missing TLS key or permission denied, re-check the Secret data key name and the env var pointing at it.

screens.title: Registering and enrolling identities with the Fabric CA
screens.narratorSegment: Once the CA is running you must register and enroll identities for Orderers and Peers so their MSPs and TLS certificates are issued. This workflow often uses the fabric-ca-client CLI, executed either from a small cli Pod inside the cluster or from a local machine that can reach the CA service. The process is: register an identity with the CA server providing a name and enrollment secret, then enroll the identity to retrieve its certificate and private key, which you will assemble into the MSP and TLS directory structures. The chapter suggests running these steps after your CA service is created and reachable via its ClusterIP service. For example, register the orderer identity, then enroll to create its certificate material and package that material into Kubernetes Secrets and ConfigMaps for distribution to Orderer Pods. A common pitfall is attempting to enroll before the CA's database and TLS files are initialized; ensure the CA logs show it is ready. Another mistake is not preserving the generated MSP/TLS files with a PVC or Secret — generated files must be persisted and mounted into the pods that need them. Key takeaway: the register/enroll cycle is the bridge between your CA and the Fabric components; perform it only after the CA reports readiness and then persist the results into Secrets or ConfigMaps for pod consumption. What identity will you enroll first in your cluster?

keyIdea.title: Enroll workflow
keyIdea.text: Register an identity on the running CA, enroll to fetch certificate material, and store MSP/TLS artifacts in Secrets/ConfigMaps for pod mounts.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › Register & Enroll
Typical steps
  1. Wait for CA readiness and obtain its service endpoint.
  2. Use fabric-ca-client to register an identity (name, type, secret).
  3. Use fabric-ca-client to enroll and retrieve the certificate and private key.
  4. Package the resulting MSP and TLS files into Secrets/ConfigMaps and mount into component pods.
Example note
Many teams run fabric-ca-client from a cli Pod within the cluster so it has network access to the CA Service and can write generated artifacts into a shared PVC for later consumption.
Pitfalls
  • Trying to enroll before CA initialization completes.
  • Failing to store the generated materials persistently.
  • Using weak RBAC so many pods can read private keys unnecessarily.
Validate enrollment artifacts by checking that the certificate files are present and the MSP and TLS folders follow Fabric's expected layout before creating the Secrets for pods.

screens.title: Raft Orderer overview and why StatefulSet
screens.narratorSegment: A Raft ordering service uses multiple Orderer nodes to reach consensus and provide fault tolerance. Raft requires stable, unique network identities and persistent ledger storage for each node. Kubernetes StatefulSets provide exactly these guarantees: stable hostnames (orderer-0, orderer-1, etc.) and per-pod persistent storage via volumeClaimTemplates. That is why StatefulSet is the preferred primitive for a Raft-based Orderer cluster. In practice you will create a StatefulSet for N replicas (commonly 3 or 5 for production), include volumeClaimTemplates so each replica has its own PVC, and pre-generate or provision cryptographic materials for each Orderer node. Another important detail is that each Orderer must be addressable by the Raft consenters list with its stable hostname and TLS certificate so the cluster can form. A misconception is assuming a Deployment can substitute for StatefulSet by adding labels; it cannot provide stable identity or per-pod PVC templates. Key takeaway: use StatefulSet for Orderers to ensure each replica retains its ledger and retains a stable identity necessary for Raft. Which component of Raft depends most critically on a stable hostname? Raft Orderer overview and why StatefulSet means use statefulsets to provide stable hostnames and per-pod pvcs — both are required for raft orderer replicas to maintain ledger continuity and form consensus.. In practical terms, raft requirements and kubernetes primitives that satisfy them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Kubernetes StatefulSets provide exactly these guarantees: stable hostnames (orderer-0, orderer-1, etc.) and per-pod persistent storage via volumeClaimTemplates. That is why StatefulSet is the preferred primitive for a Raft-based Orderer cluster. In practice you will create a StatefulSet for N replicas (commonly 3 or 5 for production), include volumeClaimTemplates so each replica has its own PVC, and pre-generate or provision cryptographic materials for each Orderer node. Another important detail is that each Orderer must be addressable by the Raft consenters list with its stable hostname and TLS certificate so the cluster can form. A misconception is assuming a Deployment can substitute for StatefulSet by adding labels; it cannot provide stable identity or per-pod PVC templates. Key takeaway: use StatefulSet for Orderers to ensure each replica retains its ledger and retains a stable identity necessary for Raft. Which component of Raft depends most critically on a stable hostname? In practical terms, raft requirements and kubernetes primitives that satisfy them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use StatefulSets to provide stable hostnames and per-pod PVCs — both are required for Raft orderer replicas to maintain ledger continuity and form consensus.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › Raft & StatefulSet
Why StatefulSet
  • Stable network identity for each Orderer replica.
  • Per-pod stable storage via volumeClaimTemplates for ledger files.
  • Ordered, graceful pod startup and termination for controlled cluster changes.
Use 3 or 5 replicas for fault tolerance; ensure consistent TLS identities and a correct consenters list when bringing up the cluster.
Misconception check
A Deployment cannot guarantee stable hostnames or produce per-pod PVCs via templates. Attempting to use a Deployment for Raft often leads to mismatched hostnames in the consenters list and ledger corruption risk.
Key Takeaway

StatefulSet semantics are necessary for Raft orderers: stable hostnames and per-replica storage are not optional for production consensus.

screens.title: StatefulSet manifest and volumeClaimTemplates for Orderers
screens.narratorSegment: When designing a StatefulSet for Orderers, the critical parts are the service that governs the StatefulSet's network identity, the StatefulSet spec with replicas and selector, and the volumeClaimTemplates that create per-pod PVCs automatically. The headless Service (ClusterIP: None) provides DNS entries for stable hostnames like orderer-0. orderer-headless. default. svc. cluster. local. The StatefulSet's volumeClaimTemplates ensure each replica gets its own PVC named something like data-orderer-orderer-0. In the container spec include env vars for ORDERER_GENERAL_LOCALMSPID, ORDERER_GENERAL_LISTENPORT, and set ORDERER_CONSENSUS_TYPE to raft. keyIdea.text: Use a headless Service plus a StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates to give each Orderer replica a stable hostname and dedicated persistent storage for its ledger.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › Orderer StatefulSet
Key YAML parts
  • Headless Service with clusterIP: None to provide stable DNS entries.
  • StatefulSet spec with replicas count and selector.
  • volumeClaimTemplates section to create a PVC per replica for ledger storage.
  • Mount pre-generated MSP/TLS via Secrets/ConfigMaps into each pod.
volumeClaimTemplates example
volumeClaimTemplates:
- metadata:
    name: orderer-ledger
  spec:
    accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
    resources:
      requests:
        storage: 5Gi
Practical notes
  • Provide genesis.block via ConfigMap or mounted volume so the Orderer can boot with the network configuration.
  • Set ORDERER_CONSENSUS_TYPE=raft and populate ORDERER_CONSENSUS_RAFT_CONSENTERS with stable hostnames and TLS cert details.
If you change replica counts, add or remove consenters carefully; Raft membership changes are sensitive and require correct TLS identities and hostnames.

screens.title: Mounting crypto materials: Secrets vs ConfigMaps
screens.narratorSegment: Cryptographic materials include private keys, certificates, and MSP folder structures, while non-sensitive artifacts include configtxgen outputs like genesis. block and channel transactions. Kubernetes Secrets are intended for sensitive data such as private keys and should be used to provide TLS keys and private signing keys to pods. ConfigMaps are suitable for non-sensitive files like genesis. block or channel configuration transactions you need to mount into Orderer pods. A practical pattern is to store private keys in Secrets, mount them read-only, and store genesis. block in a ConfigMap or an init-volume backed by a PVC. The chapter recommends pre-generating the MSP and TLS materials and then creating Secrets for each Orderer node containing its private key and cert. A common mistake is placing private keys in ConfigMaps or embedding them directly in Deployment manifests, which risks accidental exposure. Another issue is exceeding Secret size limits by placing entire directories instead of individual files; when artifacts are larger consider mounting a PVC with the files. Key takeaway: Secrets for private keys and certificate files; ConfigMaps for public configuration artifacts. Which artifact would you always put in a Secret?

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › Secrets vs ConfigMaps
Secrets
Designed for small sensitive values like private keys and certificates. Mount read-only, restrict RBAC, and avoid committing data into version control.
Use for
  • Private signing keys for CA and Orderer
  • TLS key files
ConfigMaps
Store non-sensitive configuration files such as genesis.block or channel artifacts that must be available at runtime.
Use for
  • Genesis block and channel config transactions
  • Non-sensitive config files
Practical pattern
Pre-generate MSP/TLS materials, create Secrets for private keys and certs, create ConfigMaps for genesis.block, and mount both into Orderer pods. For large directories or many files consider populating a PVC with the artifacts and mounting that instead of overloading Secrets or ConfigMaps.

screens.title: Networking and Services for Orderers
screens.narratorSegment: Networking for a Raft ordering service needs careful planning. Internally, a headless Service (clusterIP: None) provides DNS names for StatefulSet pods so raft consenters can reference stable hostnames. Many teams also create individual ClusterIP Services for each Orderer pod to simplify internal communication and to match traditional consenters references. For exposing the ordering endpoint externally to peers and client applications you may create a LoadBalancer or NodePort Service in front of a coordinating Orderer or an ingress mechanism; the chapter notes that a ClusterIP is typical for internal communication. Ensure the ORDERER_CONSENSUS_RAFT_CONSENTERS list matches the stable hostnames provided by the headless service and the TLS certificate hostnames embedded in the node certs. A common pitfall is using ephemeral IPs or external names in consenters configuration; Raft requires stable hostnames and cert matching. Validate service endpoints with kubectl get svc and DNS resolution within the cluster. Key takeaway: use a headless Service for StatefulSet stability, add per-pod services if needed for clarity, and choose an appropriate external Service type only after confirming internal consensus is healthy. How will you test that each Orderer hostname resolves correctly in the cluster?

Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › Orderer Networking
Service patterns
  • Headless Service (clusterIP: None) for stable DNS names used by StatefulSet pods.
  • Optional per-pod ClusterIP services to simplify internal addressing.
  • Expose externally using LoadBalancer or NodePort only after internal connectivity is validated.
Check
Confirm ORDERER_CONSENSUS_RAFT_CONSENTERS entries use the stable hostnames and that TLS certificate CN/SANs match those hostnames. Use kubectl exec into a test Pod and nslookup the expected hostnames to confirm DNS resolution.
Common error
Listing ephemeral pod IPs or incorrect hostnames in the consenters configuration causes Raft to fail forming a stable cluster. Ensure stable hostnames and cert alignment.

screens.title: Troubleshooting CA and Orderer deployments
screens.narratorSegment: When deployments fail the first step is to gather diagnostic information. Use kubectl get pods -l to confirm Pod states, kubectl describe pod to see mount and event errors, and kubectl logs to inspect startup messages. For CAs, look for the 'Starting CA server' log entry and errors about missing TLS key or permission denied. For Orderers, check that the genesis. block is present and that the MSP and TLS mount paths exist. A frequent cause of failure is mismatched Secret or ConfigMap names, wrong file names inside Secrets, or incorrect env vars pointing to the TLS keyfile path. For Raft specifically, verify ORDERER_CONSENSUS_RAFT_CONSENTERS contains the stable hostnames and the correct TLS certificate fingerprints or file references. Also confirm PVCs are Bound and that volume mounts are present in the Pod spec. The chapter suggests common commands: kubectl logs, kubectl describe pod, and kubectl get pvc to check binding. A typical misconception is blaming Fabric for errors that stem from Kubernetes misconfiguration; often the fix is correcting a filename, env var, or claimName. Key takeaway: methodically correlate Pod events, logs, Secret/ConfigMap names, and PVC bindings to find and fix deployment issues. keyIdea.text: Collect logs, describe pods, check PVC binding, and validate Secret/ConfigMap names and env vars to isolate CA or Orderer startup errors.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.4 › Troubleshooting
Diagnostic checklist
  1. kubectl get pods -l <label> to see pod status.
  2. kubectl describe pod <pod> to see events and mount errors.
  3. kubectl logs <pod> to read component startup messages.
  4. kubectl get pvc to confirm claims are Bound and have sufficient capacity.
Common fixes
  • Correct Secret names or data keys if TLS key file not found.
  • Ensure a StorageClass exists or manually bind a PV if PVC remains Pending.
  • Update ORDERER_CONSENSUS_RAFT_CONSENTERS to use stable hostnames matching node certs.
Example commands
kubectl get pods -l org=org1
kubectl describe pod ca-org1-xxxxx
kubectl logs orderer-0
kubectl get pvc
Use these to gather the facts before changing manifests — changing things blindly can create additional issues in a stateful cluster.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to deploy the two foundational services of a production Hyperledger Fabric network on Kubernetes: the Fabric Certificate Authority and a Raft-based Orderer cluster. We will focus on the practical Kubernetes primitives you need — Persistent Volume Claims for durability, Secrets for private keys, Deployments or StatefulSets where they belong, and Services for networking. You will see concrete YAML snippets and a live workflow for creating crypto material, encoding keys, creating Secrets, and applying manifests. Understanding these components matters because identity and ordering are the backbone of Fabric: if a CA loses its database or an Orderer loses its ledger state, the network can become inconsistent or fail. A common misconception is that everything can be ephemeral in Kubernetes; for Fabric it cannot — cryptographic materials and ledgers must be persistent and carefully handled. By the end you will know which Kubernetes object to use for each need, how to provide the CA and Orderer with their certificates, and how to validate they started correctly. Ready to explore the key topics and practical steps that follow?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to design Kubernetes manifests and deploy Fabric Certificate Authorities and a Raft-based Orderer cluster with production considerations. You will learn to persist CA and Orderer data using Persistent Volume Claims, protect private keys using Kubernetes Secrets, and choose the appropriate workload object — Deployment for a single CA instance and StatefulSet for a Raft Orderer cluster. You'll also be able to prepare and mount MSP and TLS materials using Secrets and ConfigMaps, register and enroll identities using the fabric-ca-client workflow, and validate deployments using kubectl logs and describe. For example, you will practice base64 encoding a CA private key, create the Secret manifest, apply a PVC manifest, and launch a CA Deployment that mounts both. We will also cover the genesis. block production step and how to ensure the ORDERER_CONSENSUS_RAFT_CONSENTERS list matches your StatefulSet hostnames and TLS certificates so Raft can form correctly. This competency ensures your network has durable identity management and a stable ordering backbone.

These objectives describe the hands-on skills you'll practice. First, you'll create a base64 representation of a CA private key and put it into a Kubernetes Secret so the CA Pod can access its key at runtime without embedding it in YAML. Second, you'll create a Persistent Volume Claim and mount it into the CA Pod so the CA database and generated certificates survive restarts. Third, you'll design a StatefulSet manifest for a Raft Orderer cluster that gives each pod a stable hostname and its own PVC for ledger data, crucial for consensus. Finally, you'll perform validation steps: check pods with kubectl get pods -l, inspect logs for the CA server startup message, and verify the ORDERER_CONSENSUS_RAFT_CONSENTERS list matches stable hostnames and TLS certificates. These tasks matter because they reduce downtime, prevent accidental exposure of private keys, and allow Raft to form a stable cluster. Each skill maps to an exam-style competency: persistent storage, secrets management, StatefulSet design, and troubleshooting.

A Fabric Certificate Authority issues and manages the cryptographic identities used by peers, orderers, and client applications. It maintains a database of registered identities and issues X.509 certificates when clients enroll. In Kubernetes, the CA must persist both its database and any root crypto material so that restarts do not lose identity state. Typically, a single CA instance for an organization can run as a Deployment, because it does not require a stable network identity for consensus like a Raft Orderer does. However, the CA does need persistent storage: mount a Persistent Volume Claim into the CA container at the server home path so the database and generated certs survive Pod termination. A concrete example is defining a PVC requesting 1Gi and mounting it at /etc/hyperledger/fabric-ca-server, which keeps SQLite or PostgreSQL files and the root certificate across restarts. A common misconception is that Secrets alone provide persistence; they do not — Secrets secure small pieces of data but your CA's database and generated TLS cert files require a PVC. Key takeaway: use a Deployment for CA lifecycle, PVC for persistence, and Secrets for private key handling so your CA remains both durable and secure. How will you confirm the CA retained its database after a restart?

Persistent Volume Claims are the Kubernetes primitive you use to request durable storage from the cluster. For Fabric components this is essential: CA databases and Orderer ledgers must survive Pod restarts. The typical flow is: create a PVC manifest specifying access mode and requested storage, apply it, and reference the claim in your Deployment or StatefulSet volume mounts. For a CA you might request 1Gi and mount it at /etc/hyperledger/fabric-ca-server; for each Orderer in a StatefulSet you provide a per-pod PVC for ledger files. A concrete example from our chapter shows a ca-org1-pvc. yaml requesting 1Gi and ReadWriteOnce access mode. After applying the PVC, verify it bound to a PersistentVolume with kubectl get pvc. Common mistakes include insufficient storage size, wrong accessModes, or lacking a StorageClass in the cluster, which prevents binding. Another gotcha: using a single shared PVC for multiple Orderer pods will break Raft because each Orderer needs its own dedicated ledger storage. Key takeaway: match the PVC scope to the component — shared for stateless items only, per-pod for stateful ledgers. When you create a StatefulSet for Orderers, ensure the volumeClaimTemplates produce separate PVCs for each replica.

Handling the CA private key securely is non-negotiable. The recommended pattern is to pre-generate or locate the CA's private key on a secure host, base64 encode its contents, and create a Kubernetes Secret that can be mounted as a file into the CA Pod. This keeps the key out of cleartext YAML and avoids accidental commits. The chapter provides an example workflow: find the CA private key produced by cryptogen, run a base64 encode command, and populate a Secret manifest with the resulting value. After creating the Secret, reference it in the Deployment volumes list and mount the key path into the CA server expected TLS key location. A concrete command example is to run cat | base64 -w 0 on a machine that holds the key, then place that value under data in a Secret manifest. A common slip is to place keys in ConfigMaps or in container images: neither is secure. Another mistake is failing to set the volume mount as readOnly, which increases risk. After deployment, verify the CA Pod reads the key and starts, looking for the 'Starting CA server' message in logs. Key takeaway: Secrets are the Kubernetes primitive designed for this purpose; use them with readOnly mounts and proper RBAC to restrict access. How would you confirm the Secret is mounted and used by the CA server?

A CA Deployment manifest brings together configuration, Secrets, and persistent storage. Key sections to check are metadata and labels for service selectors, env vars for FABRIC_CA_HOME and TLS configuration, ports for both CA and operations endpoints, and volumeMounts that bind the PVC and Secret to the correct paths. The example manifest in the chapter shows env vars like FABRIC_CA_SERVER_CA_NAME and FABRIC_CA_SERVER_TLS_ENABLED, ports 7054 and 9443, a PVC volume called ca-org1-data, and a secret volume for the TLS key. When you craft this manifest, confirm the secretName matches the Secret you created and that the filename inside the secret matches the env var FABRIC_CA_SERVER_TLS_KEYFILE path. Also ensure the PVC claimName matches the PVC you applied earlier. A concrete example: after applying ca-org1-deployment. yaml you should run kubectl get pods -l org=org1 and kubectl logs to confirm the CA announces it is starting. A common mistake is mismatched file names between the Secret data key and the env var pointing to the TLS keyfile; that will produce a startup error. Key takeaway: align env vars, Secret filenames, volume names, and PVC claim names precisely so the CA has the configuration and materials it expects.

Once the CA is running you must register and enroll identities for Orderers and Peers so their MSPs and TLS certificates are issued. This workflow often uses the fabric-ca-client CLI, executed either from a small cli Pod inside the cluster or from a local machine that can reach the CA service. The process is: register an identity with the CA server providing a name and enrollment secret, then enroll the identity to retrieve its certificate and private key, which you will assemble into the MSP and TLS directory structures. The chapter suggests running these steps after your CA service is created and reachable via its ClusterIP service. For example, register the orderer identity, then enroll to create its certificate material and package that material into Kubernetes Secrets and ConfigMaps for distribution to Orderer Pods. A common pitfall is attempting to enroll before the CA's database and TLS files are initialized; ensure the CA logs show it is ready. Another mistake is not preserving the generated MSP/TLS files with a PVC or Secret — generated files must be persisted and mounted into the pods that need them. Key takeaway: the register/enroll cycle is the bridge between your CA and the Fabric components; perform it only after the CA reports readiness and then persist the results into Secrets or ConfigMaps for pod consumption. A Raft ordering service uses multiple Orderer nodes to reach consensus and provide fault tolerance. Raft requires stable, unique network identities and persistent ledger storage for each node. Kubernetes StatefulSets provide exactly these guarantees: stable hostnames (orderer-0, orderer-1, etc.) and per-pod persistent storage via volumeClaimTemplates. That is why StatefulSet is the preferred primitive for a Raft-based Orderer cluster. In practice you will create a StatefulSet for N replicas (commonly 3 or 5 for production), include volumeClaimTemplates so each replica has its own PVC, and pre-generate or provision cryptographic materials for each Orderer node. Another important detail is that each Orderer must be addressable by the Raft consenters list with its stable hostname and TLS certificate so the cluster can form. A misconception is assuming a Deployment can substitute for StatefulSet by adding labels; it cannot provide stable identity or per-pod PVC templates. Key takeaway: use StatefulSet for Orderers to ensure each replica retains its ledger and retains a stable identity necessary for Raft. Mount the per-pod PVC at the ledger path and mount Secrets/ConfigMaps containing the node's MSP and TLS certs. Cryptographic materials include private keys, certificates, and MSP folder structures, while non-sensitive artifacts include configtxgen outputs like genesis. block and channel transactions. Kubernetes Secrets are intended for sensitive data such as private keys and should be used to provide TLS keys and private signing keys to pods. ConfigMaps are suitable for non-sensitive files like genesis. block or channel configuration transactions you need to mount into Orderer pods. A practical pattern is to store private keys in Secrets, mount them read-only, and store genesis. block in a ConfigMap or an init-volume backed by a PVC. The chapter recommends pre-generating the MSP and TLS materials and then creating Secrets for each Orderer node containing its private key and cert. A common mistake is placing private keys in ConfigMaps or embedding them directly in Deployment manifests, which risks accidental exposure. Another issue is exceeding Secret size limits by placing entire directories instead of individual files; when artifacts are larger consider mounting a PVC with the files. Key takeaway: Secrets for private keys and certificate files; ConfigMaps for public configuration artifacts. Which artifact would you always put in a Secret?

Networking for a Raft ordering service needs careful planning. Internally, a headless Service (clusterIP: None) provides DNS names for StatefulSet pods so raft consenters can reference stable hostnames. Many teams also create individual ClusterIP Services for each Orderer pod to simplify internal communication and to match traditional consenters references. For exposing the ordering endpoint externally to peers and client applications you may create a LoadBalancer or NodePort Service in front of a coordinating Orderer or an ingress mechanism; the chapter notes that a ClusterIP is typical for internal communication. Ensure the ORDERER_CONSENSUS_RAFT_CONSENTERS list matches the stable hostnames provided by the headless service and the TLS certificate hostnames embedded in the node certs. A common pitfall is using ephemeral IPs or external names in consenters configuration; Raft requires stable hostnames and cert matching. Validate service endpoints with kubectl get svc and DNS resolution within the cluster. Key takeaway: use a headless Service for StatefulSet stability, add per-pod services if needed for clarity, and choose an appropriate external Service type only after confirming internal consensus is healthy. When deployments fail the first step is to gather diagnostic information. Use kubectl get pods -l to confirm Pod states, kubectl describe pod to see mount and event errors, and kubectl logs to inspect startup messages. For CAs, look for the 'Starting CA server' log entry and errors about missing TLS key or permission denied. For Orderers, check that the genesis. block is present and that the MSP and TLS mount paths exist. A frequent cause of failure is mismatched Secret or ConfigMap names, wrong file names inside Secrets, or incorrect env vars pointing to the TLS keyfile path. For Raft specifically, verify ORDERER_CONSENSUS_RAFT_CONSENTERS contains the stable hostnames and the correct TLS certificate fingerprints or file references. Also confirm PVCs are Bound and that volume mounts are present in the Pod spec. The chapter suggests common commands: kubectl logs, kubectl describe pod, and kubectl get pvc to check binding. A typical misconception is blaming Fabric for errors that stem from Kubernetes misconfiguration; often the fix is correcting a filename, env var, or claimName. Key takeaway: methodically correlate Pod events, logs, Secret/ConfigMap names, and PVC bindings to find and fix deployment issues. Third, genesis. block and consenters configuration are central to bringing up the ordering service: consenters must reference stable hostnames and matching TLS certificates to form Raft clusters. Keep these three reminders close when you build or troubleshoot Fabric on Kubernetes. First, keep keys secret: place private keys in Kubernetes Secrets and mount them read-only into pods. Second, persist state correctly: use PVCs for CA databases and per-pod PVCs for Orderer ledgers created by StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplates. Third, ensure network identity alignment: the ORDERER_CONSENSUS_RAFT_CONSENTERS list, headless Service hostnames, and TLS certificate hostnames must match for Raft to reach consensus.
